utterances.text: Witness, I think you did say that you never personally saw any tanks from Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: That's correct, I never saw them personally at Trebevic, the VRS tanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from Hresa, do you know where any VRS artillery, heavy weaponry, tanks or whatever fired from into the city?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I was told that it was somewhere above Poljine, but I don't know whether they fired at the town and on which occasions they fired. I didn't see them personally so I don't know where they fired. I am not aware of this, and on which occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of VRS heavy weapons firing from Borije?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: While I was at Borije, no, there was nothing. At Borije I could have seen this. I think it must have been a little further to the north. Because of the layout of the terrain, that's why I didn't see that, I couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to the lines at the Sharpstone feature frequently or did your responsibilities take you elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: You are referring to Spicasta Stijena, the Sharpstone feature?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: The company command cause in the rear of the Sharpstone feature. It was about 200 metres at the rear. I would occasionally go there. I would occasionally go to Spicasta Stijena and visit the entire defence line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just, perhaps, Mr. Stamp, for my information, are you referring to the period when you were stationed in that area or after November 1992? It is not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This all concerns the period during which I was present in the Mrkovici area. And later I went from Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that was occasionally in -- so when you say that you would visit the entire defence line, that was during the period when you were stationed in Mrkovici, it was then that you went to Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of weapons did you -- did your company have at Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And I take it that you fired those weapons in, as I have heard before, in self-defence, in defence of your lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I think you said that -- or let me ask you instead of paraphrasing what you said. Is it correct that you or your soldiers who were along the Sharpstone feature would only fire when the opposing forces were up there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Only in order to repel attack, it was only then that we would open fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In -- I take it from your answer, "yes, absolutely," you mean that apart from that situation you would not open fire at all from Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said it was very risky to go to the edge. What made it risky?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: The enemy side were -- covered Spicasta Stijena with fire, so whoever went out to the Sharpstone feature could be killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Covered it with fire from below or from where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: From Sedrenik, the Bakija cemetery, from Sedrenik the entrance to the Sedam Suma road which leads to Mrkovici with mobile mortars, Browning at the entrance to the Sedam Suma area, the Seven Woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The mobile mortar which you speak of, did you ever see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: No, I didn't. As I said earlier on, I couldn't see it. This is information that I was provided with, but occasionally I was able to hear it being fired from very brief period of time, and from various positions. And they were indications that it was mobile, and that is the information that I had received as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You are saying it travelled through Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would it have been visible along the route that you drew on the map from Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: No. Sedrenik is not easy to see from Trebevic. A mortar on the route to Sedrenik, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could I get this clear, Witness: Are you saying that you could not see that route that you say that this vehicle travelled on from Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: No. We weren't able to see that route from our positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Did you have positions in Trebevic, on the mountain Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I heard that the Army of Republika Srpska was on Trebevic at the time that I was present there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What I am asking you now is that the route that you showed us that this vehicle is reported or was reported to you to have travelled, was that route observable from Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: It is perhaps possible to see part of the road from Trebevic, but a vehicle, a mobile vehicle transporting a mortar, no, I don't think it would be possible to identify it as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The vehicle that you heard was transporting this mortar, the intelligence information that you had in respect to it, was it available to VRS units in Trebevic, do you think or do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was available. It was available to my command, my battalion commander, but up until that time, at that time the army wasn't really well connected, the communication lines weren't very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did your unit fire at it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: No. We didn't have a position from which we would have been able to destroy such a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that there was infantry firing from Sedrenik at positions held by your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes, from part of Sedrenik, if there was fighting in the entire area of Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When fire was directed to you from Sedrenik or that part of Sedrenik, infantry fire, did your unit return the fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: While I was there there were orders and we didn't respond to those provocations unless we felt that a direct attack was being launched against us. Only in the case of a direct attack would we open fire and then there would be an intense exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you were acting according to orders that you were given?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And you would only return infantry fire into Sedrenik, if I may use your words, when you felt that a direct attack was being launched against you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And if I may paraphrase or may I quote you again, you would open fire "and then there would be an intense exchange of fire"; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please. I haven't understood you well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said only in the case of a direct attack would we open fire and then there would be an intense exchange of fire, that's what you said. That is correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From what positions did you return infantry fire into Sedrenik when it was necessary to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: The line of defence was seldom attacked in just one position. Usually it took place along the entire line. There were certain places that came under attack, but it was along the entire line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: One moment. Just simple, simply, for the sake of the economy of time. From what positions did you -- did your unit return fire into Sedrenik when you thought it was necessary to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: From along the entire line we fired on those who were attacking us, not on Sedrenik. We fired at men from the opposing side who were attacking us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask for a clarification, Witness. When you say "when they were attacking us" what do you actually mean? Do you mean soldiers coming close to your lines or would you consider mortar fire from a distance not to be part of an attack, if there was no movement of troops close to you? What exactly -- because you refer to the word "attack" several times -- what do you exactly mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "attack," and this is what took place until November 1992, they never had artillery support immediately. First the infantry would attack. So, I mean, when I say "attack," I mean they would approach our lines. They wanted to take the elevations that were of strategic importance. For us it was for defence purposes and for them it was attack purposes. So this means the Spicasta Stijena and the Mala Kula, the small fortress, so these places were of strategic importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you are talking about attacks you are talking about troops trying to move forward closest to your lines, is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you say there was an intense exchange of fire, would you mean an exchange of fire between those, I would say, first line of the BiH forces trying to move forward, or would the exchange of fire also be with those in the rear? You said you never -- you didn't fire in Sedrenik. You had exchange of fire with the, I would say, the troops in the front. When you talk about this exchange of fire, was this limited to those trying to move forward? And I am now talking about infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When there was a direct attack, yes, fire would be opened. If the exchange of fire lasted for a longer period of time, we would then ask the battalion command if we felt that we were in danger, we would ask for assistance and then they would use mortars or artillery in the positions where we were most in danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But with your own weapons, did you ever fire to any target not within this, I would say, first line or perhaps second line of the BiH forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was there, we could only use 60-millimetre mortars for a few days. We tried a Browning in Sedrenik, but we didn't have this -- we didn't have shells very often while I was there. So we used the assistance of the battalion command, we used their support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And with rifles and machine-guns, you would fire on what targets when you were attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We fired at the men who were attacking us. This area is covered by a forest. There is a forest there, so we would fire at each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that with these rifles and machine-guns you would never target anything in Sedrenik or perhaps even further away, Bakija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could only fire on Bakija from Spicasta Stijena, if we were there. But the trenches or rather the line was behind the Spicasta Stijena feature. From other positions it wasn't possible to see the Bakija and Sedrenik areas because that area is a wooded area. We -- in other areas we practically fought in the forest, both our side and their side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you say the area you are firing from was a wooded area, do I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, except in Spicasta Stijena. Apart from Spicasta Stijena, everything else was a wooded area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And from Spicasta Stijena you would have an unobstructed view there, although it was dangerous to go there, as I understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was possible to see, but it was dangerous so we were behind the rock. And if the enemy soldiers came to the rock, that is when we would fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did any of the soldiers in your unit ever get fired at when they were in the observation post at the Sharpstone feature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes, that happened, but while I was there only one man was wounded at that place. No one was killed. While I was there the observer would only go to Spicasta Stijena occasionally, and the observer wouldn't go to the most prominent point.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From the observation post, it was possible to shoot at positions in Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes. If we weren't in danger of being shot by the enemy, it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said you had two observation posts, is that so? Where was the second one, could you tell me, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: The second observation post, if you look towards the part of Sarajevo which is under Muslim control, it was to the right of the Mala Kula, about 200 metres to the right of Mala Kula, the small fortress.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Mr. President, my learned senior counsel has been -- that is the cross-examination. May it please you, Your Honours, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break anyhow. But Ms. Pilipovic, are there any questions that you would like to put to the witness in the re-examination? Yes. Then we will first adjourn until 10 minutes to 1.00 and then the Defence will have an opportunity for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher. Could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP23, you will now be further examined by counsel for the Defence. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. DP23, during the cross-examination you said that the BH Army was opening fire from a Browning at the access or the entrance to the Sedam Suma, to the Seven Woods; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little more about what is a Browning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: A Browning is an anti-aircraft machine-gun which is 12.7 millimetre calibre and it has a very long range.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "long range" do you know what it is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I can't tell you accurately. I think up to 5.000 metres, if not more.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us on the entrance to the Seven Woods, can you tell us whether from your positions, from Mala Kula, that is from the positions of your company, were you able to see this Browning, you personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes. The observer was able to see it. A Browning has a very specific sound. When it is firing, it's easy to locate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And one more question. When you were answering the question from a Presiding Judge, you said, we did not return fire in provocations, but we responded to direct attacks. Can you tell us, were you present when there were such direct attacks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes. Up to the beginning of November, I was there, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many people did you know took part in these direct attacks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: You mean from the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Were you able to assess?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Approximately 100, sometimes up to 200, maybe even more people.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Do you recall the line that you drew on one of the maps showing the path of the mobile mortar in Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown map 1801. Would you, using the pointer, show us the same path on this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Just a moment so that I can see. It was -- on the other map it was clearer. I had already indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Would you like to have a look on the other map from before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes. If I can have the previous map, it was clearer to me. I know the streets, and then it is easier. I can see it more clearly, but here on this map, I could do it approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: That one, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes. Sedrenik from the entrance to the Seven Woods, and then towards -- through Mala Sedrenik, and then to Balina Kula, that's the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: And using the other map you are not able to draw this same line? To draw the same line --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes, I can try. I can try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: It is from about here and it goes through Sedrenik, Sedrenik, that here is Mala Sedrenik and then this way to the street, Balina Kula Street, here to the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Could you mark the same line use a red pen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I can try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The line is not very visible. Please make it thicker.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I think this is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Sir, if you please, I'd like to ask you several questions for clarification purposes. The first question is in relation to your observation post at Mala Kula or near Mala Kula. Can you describe to us what was this observation post composed of, what was it like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: It was on a prominent point, and it was just beginning, so it was improvised. It was a kind of high point from which it was possible to observe the territory of the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but were you protected and by what? And your view, was it something that -- was it an open view? Were you hidden behind something? Behind a rock? A building? And how many persons could be at the same time on this observation post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: On that position there were several people. It was just on the line itself that observation post, about 5 metres in front of the first line and there was just the rampart which could protect from the fire and the view towards Ciglana and the city cemetery, the view was excellent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you -- do you mean the city cemetery of Bakija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: No. I meant the city cemetery of Bare, while Bakija is the cemetery of the Islamic religious community, that is the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, yes, it comes behind Sedrenik. You had a view of Sedrenik, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: No. From the observation post that I am talking about which looked towards the part of Sarajevo under the Muslim control -- under Muslim control, from Mala Kula to the right, you could see Ciglana, Zetra, Ciglana tunnels, Zetra, Kosevo Hospital and all the way to Mala Glava. You couldn't see anything towards Sedrenik because it is such a configuration that you couldn't see the Sedrenik area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I believe you had two observation posts. This applied to both those observation posts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes. The observation post on the Sharpstone feature, from there you couldn't see as much as you could see from the first observation post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that from your lines you were not able to see Sedrenik or Bakija or the barracks in Bakija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I am sorry. You misunderstood. From the observation post at Sharpstone it was possible to see Bakija cemetery and the barracks Bakija. That part of Sedrenik it was possible to see from the observation post at the Sharpstone, but you couldn't see it from the other observation post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am talking about both, either one or the other. I am talking about posts, observation posts. So if I understand you correctly at least from one observation post you were able to see the cemetery and the barracks in Bakija, and one part of Sedrenik. And from the other observation post you were able to see the other cemetery and the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And from these observation posts was there a possibility or at least a theoretical possibility to target, to fire, therefore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I replied to the Prosecutor. If there had been no firing, we could have fired from the Sharpstone feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, during your period or even after if you know something about this: In Sedrenik, this part, was it inhabited? Were there civilians living there or were there not civilians living there or are these kind of rear lines of the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: At the end of April in 1992 when there were clashes that were more and more frequent, that was at the end of April, the civilian population from the first lines in Sedrenik moved and sheltered into the sheltered parts. Because the soldiers were -- the troops were coming to the first front line houses, except that a gentleman, that number two that was on the piece of paper, asked me that in case that the operations continued whether he could put -- place his family in Mrkovici where my parents lived, in the depth, which is also not close to the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you correctly, there were civilians but the civilians had withdrawn, so to speak, to the rear part and they let the houses for the troops, and that was the third line, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, we are speaking about the lines of the opposing side, the first, the second and the third. You yourself, did you have one or more than one line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: On our side for the most part while I was there, there was one line and in the houses that were 2 to 300 metres behind that line, there were a certain number of troops that were -- ready in case of an attack, they would be able to come out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said that, as far as I understood, you had a Browning but that you didn't have bullets, you didn't have ammunition for it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I didn't understand what type of weapon you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am speaking about a Browning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: No, I didn't say Browning. I said we had a 60-millimetre mortar for which while we were there -- while I was there for the most part, there were no shells, and I didn't say that we had a Browning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am reading what you said in English on page 61 [In English] "We tried Browning in Sedrenik but we didn't have this, we didn't have shells very often while I was there, so we used the assistance of the battalion." [Interpretation] End of quote. So did I understand you correctly that you had a weapon of this calibre, but that perhaps you lacked ammunition or was this...?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: There was a misunderstanding. I said that Browning in Sedrenik it was controlled by the opposing side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, could you clarify this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Browning was at the entrance to the Sedam Suma to the Seven Woods on the road to Mrkovici, and this was in the hands of the opposing side. And what we did is that we asked for the assistance of the battalion to neutralise this. That's what I said. And that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. My last question is in relation to exactly what you mentioned, is that you asked for the intervention of the battalion in the event of an attack. You asked for them to help you, to be deployed. So did you mean that that would be an infantry deployment when there was an attack by the enemy side? So militarily speaking, when you were on the positions, on the line, how would you imagine this intervention? Would it be a shelling or what kind of deployment would it be? Would it be infantry deployment? How would they assist you? Where was the battalion targeting, what were the battalion's targets, in order to assist you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes. Before that I was warned, I was told that I could ask for the intervention, the assistance of the battalion. If I made an assessment that the lines of defence were certainly at risk, rather than me asking for assistance out of fear, and that's how I behaved, that's how I acted. When the lines of defence were truly at risk, when there was a risk that we would lose a line of defence, that it would fall, that's when I mostly asked for the assistance of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood, but their intervention, what was it consist of? When you say that they were intervening in the event, when the infantry troops were attacking? So if I understand there was combat, there was confrontation between two sides. So what were they targeting? What were their targets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: They fired along the line where the infantry was attacking and into the depth. For instance, the location of their Browning, the Bakija cemetery, near Karavdina house where there were mortars that were active. So as far as I know, for the most part, their task was to target those points that were putting us at risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So if I understand you correctly they would riposte, they would respond by attacking that part of Sedrenik and Bakija; is that what their intervention was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: The locations in Sedrenik where their heavy weaponry was located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they were attacking, they were targeting the heavy weapons of the other side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have got a few questions for you as well. First, a clarification in respect of your last answer. You said when you replied to a question of Judge El Mahdi: "They fired along the line where the infantry was attacking, and into the depth." And then you explained that that was the location of the Browning or the Bakija cemetery. Wasn't it risky to fire along the lines where the two opposite forces were so close to each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes. It would have been risky if they had fired at their first front line. It was assumed that we could handle that by our infantry on the first line and they would be firing on the second and on the third line and on the points where their heavy weapons were located, but not on the first line. If there was need, then an intervention unit would arrive, infantry, in order to assist because otherwise it would have been very risky for us, if they were targeting their first line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, your answer was they fired along the line where the infantry was attacking and as I heard you explain before, that was the front troops moving towards your positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I am sorry, there is a misunderstanding. They never attacked the first line. They would possibly target the second line, the closest mortars, but not the first line because that would have put us at risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the second lines, at what distance were they approximately from the first lines? If I look at what you indicated on the photographs, how much would that be, first line to the second line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: 50 to 80 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 50 to 80 metres. Were these mortar crews experienced enough to target with such precision that they would not accidently hit the first line close to where you were, but instead hit the second line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't personally know the people who manned the mortars and I don't know how they acted. It was up to me only to report to the battalion command and then someone in the battalion command relayed orders to a mortar platoon. How professional they were, I don't know. But they didn't put us in danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They didn't put you in danger, but they were targeting the second line of the BiH forces; is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I have another question in respect of the mortars of which you told us that they were fired from the Hresa area. How far would the area have been from where you were located? So, if you were either at Spicasta Stijena or at Mala Kula, how far would the Hresa area be from where mortars were fired, if you needed assistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Hresa was -- Hresa itself, it was 3 to 4 kilometers away, as the crow flies. But where the mortars were located exactly, we weren't in a position to know this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do not know the exact positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I unofficially found out that they were in the wider area of Hresa towards Crepovsko as I said, a little to the left of Hresa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By hearing, could you with a sufficient degree of certainty determine that these mortars were firing from the Hresa area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: That was when the fighting was progressing, I could hear explosions from the enemy, but shells being fired itself, no I couldn't hear that because of the action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then how could you make a distinction between 500 metres more to the west or 500 metres more to the east by just listening to the shells being fired, when they were fired at a distance of a couple of kilometers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that mortars were not fired from Mrkovici, but they were fired from the Hresa area. And as far as I -- if I understood you well, it was by hearing that you could make the distinction whether they came from the Hresa area or from other areas. My question is: How could you at a distance of a couple of kilometers make such a distinction as to the source of fire just by hearing, just by listening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: The battalion command was at Hresa, and Mrkovici is the battalion's final point. As I said, they could only be to the left of us. And there were rumours, nothing official, that they were in the area of Hresa. I don't know what the smaller places are called, I think from Hresa towards Crepovsko, that was more or less a secret that everyone knew about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, these were rumours. How -- well, you were very definite in your answer that mortars were never fired from Mrkovici. How could you be so sure about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: On several occasions fire was opened from 60-millimetre mortars. While I was there, there were no other mortars in Mrkovici, because I was born in Mrkovici. I could have seen that myself. I would have known about that. Nothing could have happened without me knowing about it. So up until the end of November, there were none in Mrkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your answer is that you never saw them and you would have seen them if they would have been there. So, it is rather a conclusion on the basis of what you observed by looking at what happened in Mrkovici than to listening to the sounds of mortars being fired; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be shown the photographs, I think they are now D1802, and 1803, two connecting photographs. And could the usher please put them so on the ELMO so that they make one. Mr. DP23, this view would be from what point, in your experience? Where would the camera have been to have this view, have this picture taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: This could have been taken from below the Spicasta Stijena to the west. I think that's where the photograph was taken from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And from that point you would have this relatively unobstructed view of not only the Sedrenik area, but also on the Old City?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: No. No. From the lines that we were positioned at, it was not possible to see this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am not asking you about your positions. But if you say this was taken from below the Spicasta Stijena, would this then be the relatively unobstructed view from a lower position where you could see the Old City and the Sedrenik area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes, from below probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: From that lower position there was no obstacle to vision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the higher position what were the obstacles? If you would go higher up, what would be the obstacles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: There was a pine wood and a layout of the terrain below. But on some of the photographs, in some of the photographs you can't see a lot of that forest. It has apparently been cut down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from the woods at a higher position, what else would obstruct the view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: The layout of the terrain itself. Where we were positioned, the layout of the terrain itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would be on the ridge of the Spicasta Stijena, would you then where the terrain, as far as I understand, would not obstruct your view any more, would you then have a similar look or if you would be at the ridge, and I do understand that the ridge was how far exactly from your positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: The most prominent position of that stone was about 20 metres from the positions and 5 metres from the observation post. We could see these houses, not these ones here. So it was possible to see this part, this part here, and then this cemetery on Grlica hill, and then the terrain -- there is a slope in the terrain and then you could see this -- these houses here. And then further on towards the barracks and the Bakija cemetery. But from here, from the cemetery --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please with your pointer go to approximately the middle of the photograph, the two photographs and indicate until what point you could -- you would have a view. So you just -- yes, from there. Could you tell us what houses you still could see and then where you could not see any more.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: We could see this part to the right, not this house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Could you please go a bit left to the left of that line you just indicated before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, approximately there. What house could you see and what house -- if you indicate the last house you would see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: To the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that a house you could still see? Please put your pointer on the photograph so that there is no -- you could still see that house? Yes? Please move it -- leave it where you were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: That.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A little bit to the left, a little bit to the left -- for example the last house with a red roof you just indicated near to that what seems to be kind of a dome. Could you -- if you look at this line, could you explain to me what would take your view more upwards on that photograph? I mean, if you could see for example that point you are just indicating, what would obstruct your view further up in the direction of the city and further up the hill at the other side of the valley? I mean, if you could see that house you are pointing at now, what would take your view --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Further up in the direction of the city?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: I understand you. The layout or the Sharpstone feature is here, and here to the left, that's where you have the Sharpstone feature. And the layout of the ground is search that our vision was obstructed from this point, the vision further afield over there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but could you explain --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: -- from that position where we were located. Only when you descended five metres down was it possible to see further away. It was important to descend 5 metres lower down. That is as far as that is concerned. But as far as this urban part of town is concerned, you have the social club here in Sedrenik, and these houses here, and there is a slope, a steep slope from these houses and it can't be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But if you go back to the social club in Sedrenik, what you just indicated, you just indicate would the pointer the social club in Sedrenik. Could you please point at it again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What could possibly obstruct the view if you could see this building from anything further in the direction of the city or to the hill at the opposite? Would that be clouds or would that be -- what would obstruct your view? I am just trying to understand why you indicate to us that you can see the buildings in the lower part of the photograph, but not anything in the higher part of the photograph. I am just trying to understand you. Why could you see the social club and why couldn't you see the buildings just further away from the social club?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: The layout was such that we could see that and then we could see the road and above the road, but the rest is a valley. The layout is a valley. The layout of the terrain prevented us from seeing certain parts. I said what you can see changes a lot. If you move 5 metres, but the layout of the terrain is that under the -- below the social club --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you couldn't see what was below the social club. That's what I understand. But what I still have difficulties in understanding is why you could not see anything which on the photograph is up from the social club. Below I understand, but from the social club up in the direction of, let's say, the other side of the valley. Why couldn't you see that if you could see the social club? That's, as a matter of fact, my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: From the observation post the club was to the right of us, from the observation post itself. The layout of the Sharpstone feature itself was such that part of our vision was obstructed. Here, there was a small hill on Spicasta Stijena itself and the pine wood. So this is what our vision -- our field of vision would look like here and here and this part of Grlica hill and up until this collection of houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you now telling us that you couldn't see the terrain closest the Spicasta Stijena? Was your view obstructed lower down or was your view obstructed further up from what you see in the photograph? Please indicate what part you could see and what part you could not see. You've drawn a line, more or less.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you see that part where your pointer is now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: This part, more or less. Perhaps not these houses here. But we could see this. There is a hill there and then we could see -- we could see this part here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, now further up in the direction of the opposite side of the valley, why couldn't you see the houses? If you move your pointer now above, just right up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, right up in the middle --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Up. This point here. I understand. Because of the layout of the terrain itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: We could see the main road here, the ring road and the part above the ring road, but everything else was not in our field of vision since the terrain is like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you call the "ring road" what road is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: The transit road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the transit road the road on the other side of the Miljacka river that leads up to the Pale direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP23
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarifications. Mr. DP23, this concludes your evidence in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming the very long way to The Hague. We are all aware what a journey it is for you, and especially for answering all the questions of both parties and the questions of the Bench as well. And I hope you have a safe trip home again. Madam Usher --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could deal with the documents, that would be fine, and otherwise we would have to wait until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document MFI.29 under seal, list of two names; D1800, map of Sarajevo marked by witness; D1799 under seal, pseudonym sheet; D347, photograph showing Hum hill; D1801, map, sniping incident 3 marked by witness; D1802, photograph P3758 marked by witness; D1803, photo P3760 marked by witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The documents are admitted into evidence. MFI-29 it says, and D1799 under seal. Perhaps just for the completeness of the transcript, I should have indicated with better precision where approximately the witness has situated the social club, I think he called it, which is a little bit just on P3760 just where the -- above the area where we found many trees and less houses, and approximately one-fourth of the left of that photograph. So a little bit right up from where we have an oval -- an oval structure in the foreground of that photograph. We will then adjourn until 9.00 tomorrow morning, same courtroom.
